nameStory: This moth earned its name from two key traits: it's one of the larger members of the spanworm moth family, and its caterpillars are particularly fond of munching on maple leaves. The 'spanworm' part comes from how the caterpillars move—they arch their backs and 'span' forward like they're measuring distances with their bodies, which is why these moths are also called 'inchworms' when they're young.
description: The Large Maple Spanworm Moth is a medium-sized brown moth with delicate, intricate patterns across its wings. With a wingspan reaching up to 2 inches, it's noticeably larger than many of its geometric moth relatives. These moths have the typical triangular resting pose of their family, holding their wings horizontally when at rest. Their earthy brown coloration helps them blend perfectly with tree bark during the day.

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Look for intricate wavy lines and geometric patterns across brown wings that feel papery-thin when gently touched

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Wingspan of 1.5-2 inches makes it noticeably larger than most other geometric moths you'll encounter

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: Wings held horizontally outward from the body in a triangular shape, pressed flat against surfaces

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Muted brown and tan tones with subtle variations that feel smooth and dusty to the touch

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Weak, fluttery flight that seems almost hesitant compared to stronger-flying moth species

habitat: You'll find these moths in mixed deciduous forests and woodland edges throughout New England, especially where maples, oaks, and birches grow together. They're also common in suburban areas with mature shade trees and can be found around fruit trees in orchards and yards. Look for them near outdoor lights at night or resting on tree bark during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, attracted to outdoor lights and tree sap. This is when mating occurs and females lay eggs on host plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time with adults most commonly seen from July through August. Caterpillars are actively feeding on tree leaves during this period.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity continues into early fall in warmer areas. Late-season caterpillars are preparing to pupate for overwintering.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active; the species overwinters as pupae in the soil or leaf litter beneath host trees.

funFact: Despite being called the 'Large Maple Spanworm,' these caterpillars are actually quite the food generalists—they'll happily munch on over a dozen different plant families, from your apple trees to your garden geraniums to wild grasses, making them one of the least picky eaters in the moth world!
confusionNotes: This moth can be confused with other brown geometric moths, but its larger size is usually the giveaway—if you can cover it with a quarter, it's probably something else. Remember: 'Large' is in the name for a reason, and the intricate wavy line patterns are more complex than most of its smaller cousins.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you into thinking these moths only eat maples—that's just where they were first commonly noticed. The 'geometric' family name comes from the mathematical precision of their wing patterns and their caterpillars' measuring-worm movement, not from any actual geometry skills.
compareHints: As the only Prochoerodes species commonly found in New England, compare it to other large geometric moths in the region. It's distinguished from similar brown moths by its specific combination of size, horizontal wing posture, and the particular wavy line patterns that create an almost wood-grain appearance across the wings.
